fields.Back: To retrieve a resource without causing side effects. Safe (no server state change) and idempotent; no request body.
To create a new resource or trigger a non-idempotent action (e.g. submit an order). Not safe, not guaranteed idempotent — repeating it can create duplicates.
To replace a resource entirely at a known URI. Idempotent: sending the same PUT twice leaves the resource in the same state as sending it once.
To apply a partial update to a resource (only the changed fields). Not guaranteed idempotent — depends on how the server implements the patch.
To remove the resource at a given URI. Idempotent: deleting an already-deleted resource still leaves it gone.

fields.Front: What status code should a successful POST that creates a new resource return?
fields.Back: 201 Created (often with a Location header pointing to the new resource).

fields.Front: What status code means the request succeeded but there is no body to send back (e.g. a successful DELETE)?
What's the difference between 401 Unauthorized and 403 Forbidden?
fields.Back: 401 = the request lacks valid authentication ("who are you?"). 403 = the server knows who you are but you don't have permission for this resource ("you can't do that").

fields.Front: What does a 429 status code indicate?
fields.Back: Too Many Requests — the client has exceeded a rate limit and should back off/retry later (often per a Retry-After header).

fields.Front: What are the main components you configure on a request in Postman?
fields.Back: Method + URL, query Params, Headers, Body (raw/JSON/form-data), and Authorization.

fields.Front: In Postman, what's the difference between a Collection and an Environment?
fields.Back: A Collection groups related requests together (plus their scripts/tests, run in sequence). An Environment holds a set of variables (base URL, tokens, IDs) that requests reference, so you can switch the same collection between dev/staging/prod by swapping environments.

fields.Front: Write a Postman test script asserting the response status code is 200.
Write a Postman test script asserting the JSON response body has an id property.
fields.Back:
pm.test("Response has id property", function () {
    const json = pm.response.json();
    pm.expect(json).to.have.property("id");
});

fields.Front: How do you save a value from a Postman response (e.g. an auth token) into an environment variable for later requests to use?
fields.Back:
pm.environment.set("token", pm.response.json().token);
Later requests can then reference it as {{token}}.

fields.Front: What's the difference between Bearer Token auth and Basic auth?
fields.Back: Basic auth sends a base64-encoded username:password on every request. Bearer auth sends a previously-issued token (e.g. JWT from OAuth/login) in the Authorization header, without resending raw credentials each time.

fields.Front: In Postman, what are pre-request scripts used for?
fields.Back: JavaScript that runs before the request is sent — e.g. computing a timestamp/signature, generating dynamic test data, or setting an auth header/variable that the request needs.
Making the identical request multiple times leaves the server in the same state as making it once. GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent; POST is not.

fields.Text: HTTP status codes are grouped by their first digit: {{c1::2xx}} = success, {{c2::3xx}} = redirection, {{c3::4xx}} = client error, {{c4::5xx}} = server error.
